mainTopic: Dating documents by the Greek kings, and the meaning of יום גינוסיא, with stories of אנטונינוס and רבי
overview: The talmidim of רבה saw a שטר whose date seemed six years too late, and they wanted to treat it as a שטר מאוחר. רב נחמן said a precise scribe wrote it, counting the six years the Greeks ruled only in עילם, and a ברייתא of רבי יוסי backs him up. רב אחא בר יעקב asked why the scribe could not have counted from יציאת מצרים, but a ברייתא confirms that in the גולה years are counted only by the Greek kings. רבינא adds a proof from the משנה in ראש השנה: documents today start the year in תשרי, the way the years of non-Jewish kings are counted, and not in ניסן as a count from יציאת מצרים would. The גמרא then asks what יום גינוסיא in our משנה means. After trying 'birthday' and testing several ברייתות, it settles on the king's coronation day, either his own or his son's. To show that a king's son can be crowned, the גמרא tells how אנטונינוס, advised by רבי through acted-out signs, got his son אסוירוס made king. A second story shows רבי teaching him to deal with his enemies one at a time.

steps.title: The Sages think the document is postdated
steps.stepSummary: A שטר has a date six years later than expected, so the Sages before רבה want to treat it as a שטר מאוחר and hold it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: The document said 'six extra years.' The Sages sitting before רבה thought: this is a postdated document. Let us hold it until its date arrives, so the lender will not seize property with it before then.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a real case: a document's date is six years later than it should be. The Sages before רבה say this is a שטר מאוחר and should be held until its date comes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שטר מאוחר may only be used to collect from the date written on it. If the lender used it now, he could take property the borrower sold before that date, which would be unfair to the buyers. So the Sages want to freeze the document until its date arrives.

keyTerms.meaning: A postdated document: its written date is later than the day it was really written
He seizes (collects property, especially from buyers)

phrases.english: 'Six extra years'
phrases.notes: This is the end of the case quoted just before: a document whose date was six years later than the normal count.

phrases.english: The Sages before Rabba thought to say:
This is a postdated document,
let us hold it until its time arrives
so that he will not seize property.
phrases.notes: He means the lender should not take property the borrower sold before the written date.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Sages before רבה proposed treating a document dated six years too late as a שטר מאוחר and holding it until its date arrives. רב נחמן rejects this in the next step.

steps.title: An exacting scribe counted the years in עילם
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says the document is not postdated. A precise scribe counted the six years the Greeks ruled in עילם, years most people leave out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: an exacting scribe wrote this document. There were six years when the Greeks ruled only in עילם. We do not count them, but he does. So he wrote the correct date.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן rejects the Sages' idea that this is a שטר מאוחר. He explains that the scribe simply used an earlier starting point for the Greek count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Sages assumed everyone starts counting from the same year. רב נחמן points out that a precise scribe starts six years earlier, from when the Greeks ruled in עילם. So the extra six years are not a mistake or a trick, and the document is dated correctly.

keyTerms.meaning: Elam, a land where the Greeks ruled before their rule spread everywhere

steps.whyThisMatters: The same date can mean different things depending on how the scribe counts the years, so a court must check the counting system before calling a document postdated.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: הַאי סָפְרָא דַּוְקָנָא כַּתְבֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said: An exacting scribe wrote this,
and those six years when they ruled in Elam,
which we do not count,
he does count them,
phrases.notes: Some versions say לֵיהּ ('it'); the corrected wording in square brackets is לְהוּ ('them'), meaning the years.

phrases.english: and he wrote it at its proper time.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: הַאי סָפְרָא דַּוְקָנָא כַּתְבֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the Sages' assumption that the six extra years show the document is postdated.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the conclusion that this is a שטר מאוחר.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The Sages assumed all scribes start the Greek count at the same point. A precise scribe includes the six years of rule in עילם.

steps.title: A ברייתא proves the six years in עילם
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי in a ברייתא teaches that the Greeks ruled six years in עילם before their rule spread to the whole world.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: רבי יוסי says: they ruled six years in עילם, and afterward their kingdom spread over the entire world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רב נחמן's claim that there really were six years of Greek rule in עילם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's answer depends on a historical fact. The ברייתא of רבי יוסי confirms there were two possible starting points six years apart: rule in עילם, and then rule over the whole world. That explains exactly the six-year gap.

phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Yosei says:
They ruled six years in Elam,
and afterward their kingdom spread
over the entire world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב נחמן's explanation in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That there were six years of Greek rule in עילם before it spread worldwide.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in the name of רבי יוסי.

steps.title: Maybe the scribe counted from יציאת מצרים
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב asks how we know the scribe counted by Greek rule. Maybe he counted from יציאת מצרים and left off the first thousand years, and then the document really is postdated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר יעקב objected: How do we know we count by the Greek kingdom? Maybe we count from יציאת מצרים, and the scribe dropped the first thousand and kept the second thousand. Then this document is postdated!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר יעקב challenges רב נחמן's answer. He suggests a different counting system that would make the document postdated after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's answer only works if the scribe was counting by Greek rule. If the scribe counted from יציאת מצרים and wrote only the last digits, the number could match without coming from the Greek count. Then the six-year gap is a real problem, and the document is a שטר מאוחר.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it (raises a strong challenge)

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov objects to it:
From where do we know that we count by the Greek kingdom?
Perhaps we count from the Exodus from Egypt,
and he left out the first thousand
and kept the last thousand,
phrases.notes: The Exodus count runs a thousand years ahead of the Greek count, so writing only the last digits could look like a Greek date.

phrases.english: and this one is postdated!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the assumption behind רב נחמן's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's claim that the scribe was counting by Greek rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another counting system (from יציאת מצרים, without the thousands) could produce the same number, and then the document would be postdated.

steps.title: In the גולה we count only by Greek kings
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that in the גולה people count years only by the Greek kings.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: in the גולה we count only by the Greek kings.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers the challenge by stating the accepted practice: outside ארץ ישראל, documents are dated only by Greek rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא בר יעקב's other system is ruled out because nobody in the גולה uses it. That leaves only the Greek count, so רב נחמן's explanation of the six years holds up.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: בַּגּוֹלָה אֵין מוֹנִין
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said: In the exile we do not count
except by the Greek kings alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: בַּגּוֹלָה אֵין מוֹנִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא בר יעקב's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: States the established practice that rules out the alternative counting system.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The scribe might have counted from יציאת מצרים, making the document postdated.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the גולה the only count is by the Greek kings, so the document is dated correctly.

steps.title: רב אחא checks and finds a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב thought רב נחמן was just brushing him off, but he looked into it and found a ברייתא that says exactly what רב נחמן said.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thought: he is just pushing me away. He went out, looked carefully, and found that it is taught in a ברייתא: in the גולה we count only by the Greek kings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us רב אחא בר יעקב doubted the answer at first, then found a ברייתא proving רב נחמן right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's answer sounded like a short reply with no source behind it. The ברייתא shows it is an established teaching, word for word. So רב נחמן's view holds, and in the next steps רבינא brings further support from a משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: He is just pushing him away (brushing off the question)
He went out, examined carefully, and found

steps.whatToRemember: A document dated six years later than expected is not automatically a שטר מאוחר. A precise scribe may count Greek rule from its start in עילם, and in the גולה years are counted only by the Greek kings.

phrases.aramaic: הוּא סָבַר דַּחוֹיֵי קָא מְדַחֵי לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: He thought that he was just pushing him away,
phrases.notes: רב אחא בר יעקב thought רב נחמן was giving a quick answer just to end the argument.

phrases.english: he went out, examined, and found,
as it is taught: In the exile we do not count
except by the Greek kings alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא סָבַר דַּחוֹיֵי קָא מְדַחֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms רב נחמן's answer from step 5 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That in the גולה years are counted only by the Greek kings.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא found by רב אחא בר יעקב.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב נחמן's answer stands, and the document is not postdated.

steps.title: רבינא opens a proof from the משנה about ניסן
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the משנה also shows we count by the Greek kings. He begins by quoting the line that ניסן is the New Year for kings, which רב חסדא says is about documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The משנה also shows this. We learned: 'The first of ניסן is the New Year for kings and for the festivals.' We asked what 'for kings' is for, and רב חסדא said it is for dating documents.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא starts a new proof for רב נחמן's claim. This step only sets up the first piece. The proof comes together in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא points to the משנה at the start of ראש השנה. According to רב חסדא, 'ניסן is the New Year for kings' is a rule about how dates on documents are counted. Keep this in mind, because a second line of the same משנה will seem to clash with it.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה is also precise, meaning a close reading of it supports this point
The New Year for counting kings' years
For what halacha? What practical difference does it make?
Legal documents, such as loan notes, which carry a date

phrases.english: Ravina said: The Mishnah is also precise (and shows this),
as we learned:
phrases.notes: This is the first משנה of ראש השנה, on דף 2a.

phrases.english: "On the first of Nisan is the New Year
for kings and for the festivals,"
and we said: 'For kings' — for what halacha?
phrases.notes: 'We said' points to the גמרא in ראש השנה, which asks about this משנה.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: For documents.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second support, from a משנה, for רב נחמן's claim that the גולה counts by Greek kings
steps.raayaObject: That documents are dated by the Greek kings
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה ראש השנה 2a with רב חסדא's explanation

steps.title: The תשרי line seems to contradict the ניסן line
steps.stepSummary: The same משנה says תשרי is the New Year for years. רב חסדא says that is also about documents. So the two lines about documents contradict each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: We also learned: 'The first of תשרי is the New Year for years and for שמיטה.' We asked what 'for years' is for, and רב חסדא said it is for documents. So the two rulings about documents contradict each other!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא is retelling the contradiction that the גמרא in ראש השנה raised. It is still part of his setup.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא linked both ניסן and תשרי to documents. A document's year cannot begin in two different months, so the two rulings clash. How this clash is resolved is what will prove רבינא's point.

phrases.english: And we learned: On the first of Tishrei is the New Year
for years and for Shemitah cycles,
and we said: 'For years' — for what halacha?
And Rav Chisda said: For documents.
The rulings on documents contradict each other!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the second line of the משנה, which clashes with the first
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's two explanations about documents
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Documents cannot have their year start in both ניסן and תשרי

steps.title: Jewish kings are counted from ניסן, other kings from תשרי
steps.stepSummary: The contradiction is resolved. Jewish kings' years are counted from ניסן, and the years of kings of the nations are counted from תשרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: We resolved it: one line is about Jewish kings, the other is about the kings of the nations. For the kings of the nations we count from תשרי, and for Jewish kings we count from ניסן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא repeats the answer given in ראש השנה. Both lines are about documents, but they apply to two different kinds of kings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no real contradiction. The ניסן line is for documents dated by Jewish kings, and the תשרי line is for documents dated by kings of the nations. This sets up a test: whichever month we start from today tells us which kind of count we are using.

keyTerms.meaning: Kings of the nations of the world (non-Jewish kings)

phrases.english: And we resolved it: here it is for the kings of Israel,
here it is for the kings of the nations of the world.
For the kings of the nations we count from Tishrei,
for the kings of Israel we count from Nisan.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְשַׁנֵּינַן: כָּאן לְמַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, כָּאן לְמַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each line applies to a different kind of king
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both lines give a starting month for the same kind of document date
steps.terutzMaskana: ניסן is for Jewish kings and תשרי is for kings of the nations

steps.title: Counting from תשרי shows we do not count from יציאת מצרים
steps.stepSummary: Today documents are dated from תשרי. If we counted from יציאת מצרים, the year would start in ניסן. So we must be counting by the Greek kings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, we count from תשרי. If you thought we count from יציאת מצרים, we would have to count from ניסן! So doesn't this prove that we count by the Greek kings?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא finishes his proof. He uses the month our year starts in to show which count we use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יציאת מצרים happened in ניסן, so a count from it would start in ניסן, just as Jewish kings are counted. Our documents start the year in תשרי, which is the way kings of the nations are counted. That fits counting by the Greek kings, and it answers רב אחא בר יעקב's suggestion from step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: If it would enter your mind (if you were to think)

phrases.english: And we nowadays count from Tishrei,
and if it would enter your mind
that we count from the Exodus from Egypt —
we would need to count from Nisan!
Rather, isn't it proven from this
that we count by the Greek kings?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the ניסן/תשרי split to today's way of dating documents
steps.raayaObject: That the גולה dates documents by the Greek kings, not from יציאת מצרים
steps.raayaSupportSource: Today's practice of starting the year in תשרי, together with the rule from step 9

steps.title: The גמרא accepts the proof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees: we count by the Greek kings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts רבינא's proof. This closes the discussion about how documents are dated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since documents are dated by the Greek kings, רב נחמן's view stands. A document that seems six years too late may just have been written by a precise scribe who counted the years the Greeks ruled in עילם, so it is not a postdated document.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it, meaning yes, it is proven

steps.whatToRemember: In the גולה, documents are dated by the Greek kings, and the year starts in תשרי. So a document that seems six years late can be explained by a precise scribe who counted the six years in עילם.

phrases.english: Learn from it (yes, it is proven).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the proof from step 10
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Documents are dated by the Greek kings, which supports רב נחמן's reading of the document

steps.title: What does 'the day of גינוסיא of their kings' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a phrase from the משנה and asks what it means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And the day of גינוסיא of their kings, etc.' What is 'the day of גינוסיא of their kings'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new phrase in the משנה's list of non-Jewish holidays and asks what the strange word גינוסיא means. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists days when doing business with idol worshippers is forbidden. The word גינוסיא is not a Hebrew word, so the גמרא needs to define which day it is.

keyTerms.meaning: A special celebration day connected to the king. The גמרא is trying to define it.
Their kings, meaning the kings of the nations.
Etc. The rest of the משנה's line is not quoted.
What is? Used to ask for a definition.

phrases.english: And the day of geinuseya of their kings, etc.
What is "the day of geinuseya of their kings"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of dating documents by the Greek kings.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the term יום גינוסיא in the משנה.

steps.title: רב יהודה: it is the day the king is crowned
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that יום גינוסיא is the day the nations appoint their king.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: It is the day on which the nations set up their king.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question. He says גינוסיא is coronation day, when the king is put on the throne.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the first definition. It ties the holiday to the moment the king takes power. This definition is about to be tested against a ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: They set up, meaning they appoint or crown a king.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:

phrases.aramaic: יוֹם שֶׁמַּעֲמִידִין בּוֹ גּוֹיִם אֶת מַלְכָּם.
phrases.english: The day on which the nations set up their king.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: יום גינוסיא is the day the king is crowned.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists גינוסיא and coronation day separately
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא names both 'the day of גינוסיא' and 'the day they appoint their king,' so they must be two different days.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: 'The day of גינוסיא, and the day on which they set up their king!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יהודה with a ברייתא. The ברייתא counts גינוסיא and coronation day as two separate items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If גינוסיא were the same as coronation day, the ברייתא would not list them separately. So it looks like רב יהודה's definition cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the משנה that was not included in the משנה.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: יוֹם גִּינּוּסְיָא וְיוֹם שֶׁמַּעֲמִידִין בּוֹ אֶת מַלְכָּם!
phrases.english: The day of geinuseya, and the day on which they set up their king!
phrases.notes: The word 'and' is the problem. It makes these sound like two different days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יהודה's definition from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's claim that גינוסיא is coronation day.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lists the two separately, so they cannot be the same day.

steps.title: The king's own coronation versus his son's
steps.stepSummary: One day is the coronation of the king himself, and the other is the coronation of his son.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about his own coronation, and that one is about his son's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב יהודה. Both days are coronation days, but for two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גינוסיא is the king's own coronation day. 'The day they appoint their king' in the ברייתא is the day his son is crowned. That is why the ברייתא lists two days.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. Introduces an answer.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This is his own, that is his son's.
phrases.notes: He means the king's own coronation day and his son's coronation day.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא דִידֵיהּ, הָא דִּבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case into two people: the king and his son.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's two days seemed to rule out coronation as the meaning of גינוסיא.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are coronation days. One is for the king and one is for his son.

steps.title: רב יוסף: they do not crown a king's son
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף taught from a פסוק that they do not crown the son of a king, so the 'son's coronation' answer fails.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do they really crown a king who is the son of a king? But רב יוסף taught: 'Behold, I made you small among the nations' means that they do not seat a king who is the son of a king. 'You are greatly despised' means that they have neither their own script nor their own language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 15. According to רב יוסף, a king's son is never crowned, so there is no 'son's coronation day.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 needed the son to be crowned. רב יוסף reads the פסוק in עובדיה as saying this nation's kingship does not pass from father to son. The second half about script and language is part of the same teaching and is quoted along with it.

keyTerms.meaning: And do they really set up? A question that doubts the previous claim.
A king who is the son of a king.
Script and language, meaning their own writing system and their own tongue.

phrases.english: And do they set up a king who is the son of a king?
But didn't Rav Yosef teach:
"Behold, I made you small among the nations"
meaning that they do not seat a king who is the son of a king;
"You are greatly despised"

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין לָהֶן לֹא כְּתָב וְלֹא לָשׁוֹן.
phrases.english: meaning that they have neither script nor language.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the second coronation day is the son's coronation.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a king's son is never crowned, there can be no 'son's coronation day.'

steps.title: A new definition: גינוסיא is the birthday
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the coronation idea and says יום גינוסיא is the king's birthday.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what is the day of גינוסיא? It is the birthday.
steps.whatsHappening: Because the coronation answer ran into trouble, the גמרא gives a completely new meaning: the king's birthday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Rather' tells us the earlier explanation is being dropped. With גינוסיא as the birthday, the ברייתא from step 14 is no problem, because coronation day and birthday really are two different days.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. Signals dropping the earlier answer for a new one.
The day of birth, a birthday.

phrases.english: Rather, what is the day of geinuseya?
The birthday.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to step 16 by replacing the definition.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists גינוסיא and birthday separately
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא lists 'the day of גינוסיא' and 'the birthday' as two items, so they cannot be the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: 'The day of גינוסיא, and the birthday!'
steps.whatsHappening: The new answer meets the same kind of problem as the first one. A ברייתא counts גינוסיא and the birthday separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works exactly like step 14. The ברייתא's separate listing shows that גינוסיא is not the birthday.

keyTerms.meaning: And the day. Here the 'and' marks a separate item in the list.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a baraita:
The day of geinuseya, and the birthday!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the birthday definition of step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that גינוסיא is the birthday.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lists the two separately, so they cannot be the same day.

steps.title: The king's own birthday versus his son's
steps.stepSummary: One is the king's own birthday, and the other is his son's birthday.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is his own birthday, and that one is his son's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the same split as before, now for birthdays. גינוסיא is the king's birthday, and 'the birthday' in the ברייתא is his son's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's problem does not apply here. A son has a birthday whether or not he will ever be crowned.

keyTerms.meaning: This one ... that one. Used to divide two cases.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This is his own, that is his son's.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דִידֵיהּ, הָא דִּבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case into two people: the king and his son.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to rule out birthday as the meaning of גינוסיא.
steps.terutzMaskana: גינוסיא is the king's birthday, and the other birthday is his son's.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists four days: גינוסיא and birthday for both king and son
steps.stepSummary: A fuller ברייתא lists גינוסיא for the king and his son, and also birthdays for the king and his son, so גינוסיא cannot be any birthday.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: 'His day of גינוסיא, his son's day of גינוסיא, his birthday, and his son's birthday!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that already splits everything between king and son. This defeats the birthday answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 said 'the birthday' was the son's birthday. This ברייתא lists the king's birthday and the son's birthday separately from both גינוסיא days. So גינוסיא is not a birthday of anyone.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: יוֹם גִּינּוּסְיָא שֶׁלּוֹ, יוֹם גִּינּוּסְיָא שֶׁל בְּנוֹ,
phrases.english: His day of geinuseya, his son's day of geinuseya,

phrases.aramaic: וְיוֹם הַלֵּידָה שֶׁלּוֹ, וְיוֹם הַלֵּידָה שֶׁל בְּנוֹ!
phrases.english: and his birthday, and his son's birthday!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defeats the answer of step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The birthday definition, even with the king and son split.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both birthdays already appear in the list apart from both גינוסיא days, so גינוסיא cannot be a birthday.

steps.title: Back to the first answer: coronation day, the king's own and his son's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to coronation day and again explains the double listing as the king's own day and his son's.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what is 'the day of גינוסיא'? The day they set up their king. And it is not difficult: this one is his own, and that one is his son's.
steps.whatsHappening: Since birthday has been ruled out, the גמרא goes back to רב יהודה's original definition, the coronation day. It answers the ברייתא of step 14 with the same split as in step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fuller ברייתא of step 20 itself speaks of a גינוסיא 'of his son.' So the גמרא returns to coronation day and again divides it into the king's own coronation and his son's.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is not difficult. Here it brings back an answer that was used earlier.

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a third new definition. It is exactly רב יהודה's answer from step 13, with the same king and son split from step 15.
steps.whatToRemember: יום גינוסיא is the king's coronation day. When a ברייתא lists it next to another coronation day, one is the king's own and the other is his son's.

phrases.english: Rather, what is "the day of geinuseya"?
The day on which they set up their king;
and it is not difficult:
this is his own, that is his son's.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַאי ״יוֹם גִּינּוּסְיָא״? יוֹם שֶׁמַּעֲמִידִין בּוֹ מַלְכָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 by returning to the definition of step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Returning to the earlier definition and reusing the king and son split.
steps.terutzMaskana: גינוסיא is coronation day, either the king's own or his son's.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: יום גינוסיא means the king's coronation day.

steps.title: A king's son can become king if the king asks for it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא heads off a question on the coronation explanation. The Romans do appoint a king's son as king when the king requests it, as happened with אסוירוס son of אנטונינוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it bothers you that the Romans do not appoint a king's son as king, they do appoint him through a request, like אסוירוס son of אנטונינוס, who ruled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא expects you to ask how the son of a king could have a coronation day, since Romans don't make a king's son king. It answers that this does happen when the king asks for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 explained the double listing as the coronation day of the king and the coronation day of his son. That clashes with the earlier claim that Romans don't crown a king's son. The answer is that the usual practice has an exception: the son can be crowned at his father's request.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it is difficult for you. The גמרא uses this to answer a question before you ask it.
אסוירוס, son of the Roman emperor אנטונינוס

phrases.english: And if it is difficult for you
that they do not appoint as king the son of a king,
through a request they do appoint him,
for example, Asveirus son of Antoninus, who ruled.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי קַשְׁיָא לָךְ דְּלָא מוֹקְמִי מַלְכָּא בַּר מַלְכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends step 21's answer (the king's coronation day and his son's) against a possible objection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the earlier rule: a king's son is not normally crowned, but he is crowned when the king requests it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Romans never crown a king's son, so a son's coronation day could not exist.
steps.terutzMaskana: A king's son can be crowned at his father's request, so a son's coronation day is possible.

steps.title: אנטונינוס asks רבי how to get two favors from the Senate
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס tells רבי he wants two things: his son crowned in his place, and טבריא freed from taxes. The Senate will grant him only one request.
steps.simpleTranslation: אנטונינוס said to רבי: I want my son אסוירוס to rule in my place, and I want טבריא made a tax-free city. If I ask them for one thing, they do it. If I ask for two, they don't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins the background story behind the example of אסוירוס. אנטונינוס brings רבי a problem: he wants two favors but can only ask for one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story shows how אסוירוס came to rule through his father's request, which supports step 22. The problem is set up clearly: two wishes, but a limit of one request.

keyTerms.meaning: A Roman emperor who was a friend of רבי
A colony, meaning a city freed from paying taxes

phrases.english: Antoninus said to Rebbi:
I want Asveirus my son to rule in my place,
and that Tiberias be made a free city,
phrases.notes: A קָלָנְיָא was a city that didn't have to pay taxes to Rome.

phrases.english: and if I tell them one thing, they do it,
two, they do not do it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַנְטוֹנִינוּס לְרַבִּי בָּעֵינָא דְּיִמְלוֹךְ אַסְוִירוּס בְּרִי תְּחוֹתַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the background story for the example of אסוירוס in step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can אנטונינוס get both his son crowned and טבריא freed from taxes when the Senate grants only one request?

steps.title: The dove on the shoulders: ask for one thing, and let your son do the other
steps.stepSummary: רבי answers by acting it out. One man stands on another holding a dove, and the bottom man tells the top man to release it. אנטונינוס understands the message: ask the Senate only to crown his son, then have his son free טבריא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי brought a man and put him on his friend's shoulders. He gave a dove to the one on top and told the one on the bottom: tell the one on top to let the dove fly from his hand. אנטונינוס said: this must be what he is telling me. Ask them to let אסוירוס my son rule in my place, and then tell אסוירוס to make טבריא a free city.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי answers without words by acting out a scene. אנטונינוס works out what it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bottom man is אנטונינוס, the top man is his son, and the dove is the tax-free status of טבריא. אנטונינוס uses his one request on crowning his son. The son, once he is king, grants the second favor himself. This also confirms step 22: אסוירוס became king because his father asked.

keyTerms.meaning: He mounted him on his fellow's shoulders
The upper one / the lower one
Learn from this; this must mean

steps.whyThisMatters: The story shows a real case where a king's son was crowned at his father's request. That supports the explanation that a son's coronation day could be one of the Roman holidays.

phrases.english: He brought a man, and mounted him on his fellow,
phrases.notes: "He" is רבי, who answers by acting it out instead of speaking.

phrases.english: and gave a dove to the upper one (in his hand),
phrases.notes: The words in round brackets are in the printed גמרא, but the corrected wording leaves them out.

phrases.english: and he said to the lower one:

phrases.aramaic: אֵימַר (לעילא דלמפרח) [לְעִילַּאי דְּנַפְרַח] יוֹנָה מִן יְדֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Tell the upper one to make the dove fly from his hand.
phrases.notes: The words in round brackets are the printed wording, and the words in square brackets are the corrected wording. Both mean the same thing.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ הָכִי קָאָמַר לִי:
phrases.english: He said: Learn from this, this is what he is telling me:
phrases.notes: Now "he" is אנטונינוס, working out the meaning to himself.

phrases.english: You ask of them
that "Asveirus my son should rule in my place,"
and tell Asveirus
that he should make Tiberias a free city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem אנטונינוס raised in step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Use the one request to have your son crowned, and then let your son grant the second favor himself.

steps.title: אנטונינוס complains that powerful Romans trouble him
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס brings רבי a second problem: important Romans are giving him trouble.
steps.simpleTranslation: אנטונינוס said to רבי: important Romans are troubling me.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues with a second request for advice. This line only sets up the problem, and רבי's answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new problem, not part of the question about crowning. The גמרא keeps telling stories about how רבי advised אנטונינוס.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מְצַעֲרִין לִי חֲשִׁיבִי רוֹמָאֵי.
phrases.english: He said to him: Important Romans are troubling me.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מְצַעֲרִין לִי חֲשִׁיבִי רוֹמָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about אנטונינוס asking רבי for advice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How should אנטונינוס deal with the powerful Romans who trouble him?

steps.title: The radishes in the garden: deal with enemies one at a time
steps.stepSummary: רבי takes אנטונינוס into his garden and pulls up one radish each day. אנטונינוס understands: get rid of his enemies one by one, not all at once.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי would bring him into the garden, and every day he pulled up one radish from the garden bed in front of him. אנטונינוס said: this must be what he is telling me. Kill them one at a time, and don't provoke all of them at once.
steps.whatsHappening: Again רבי answers by acting instead of speaking, and אנטונינוס works out the meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pulling only one radish a day shows the method. If you remove enemies slowly, the rest don't unite against you. Fighting all of them at once would turn them all against you together.
steps.whatToRemember: Both stories follow the same pattern. רבי answers אנטונינוס by acting out the advice instead of saying it, and אנטונינוס works out what it means. The first story also backs up the point that a king's son could be crowned at his father's request.

phrases.english: He would bring him into the garden,
phrases.notes: The words in round brackets are the printed wording, and the words in square brackets are the corrected wording. "He" is רבי.

phrases.english: every day he uprooted a radish
from the garden bed in front of him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ הָכִי קָאָמַר לִי —
phrases.english: He said: Learn from this, this is what he is telling me:
You kill them one at a time,
and do not provoke all of them at once.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the complaint אנטונינוס raised in step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Remove the troublesome nobles one at a time, so they never band together against you.
